tier_reason: First-party commit message (41b6106, 9 Jun 2013) with four single ~1 s runs of the public tests/bench/iopipes.c harness (-n 1024 -c 1, with -e for libevent); compiler, flags, CPU model and libevent version are not stated, so it falls short of A and is not independent.

corrections.workload: tests/bench/iopipes.c (iopipes.t) event-dispatch benchmark: 1024 AF_UNIX socketpairs (-n 1024), each primed with one byte; every read callback reads the byte and writes one back, so each descriptor stays permanently ready, and the tool counts callbacks dispatched per second over a ~1 s run on one scheduler thread (-c 1). libphenom re-arms with ph_job_set_nbio; the libevent mode (-e) uses the legacy event_init/event_set API with non-persistent EV_READ events re-added via event_add in every callback.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Commit 41b6106 'Streamline nbio scheduling a bit' (9 Jun 2013): 'we're a bit faster because we're doing overall less book keeping per event'. Linux, './tests/bench/iopipes.t -n 1024 -c 1': libphenom 366,624 events/s vs libevent ('-e') 264,129 events/s (about 1.39x, derived from page data). OSX: libphenom 505,155 events/s vs libevent 471,385 events/s (about 1.07x, derived from page data). The OSX and Linux boxes are different machines; single core only because that is all the harness can compare against libevent.
corrections.caveats: First-party, single ~1 s runs from one commit message in June 2013; hardware, compiler, flags and libevent version are all unstated, and OSX and Linux numbers came from different machines. The commit added the -e option 'so that it is simpler to gut check against it'. The libevent side of the harness uses the deprecated libevent 1.x API (event_init/event_set) with non-persistent events re-added after every callback rather than EV_PERSIST, which probably costs libevent's epoll backend extra epoll_ctl calls per event, while the same commit makes libphenom track kernel descriptor state to avoid syscalls; libevent is therefore not shown at its fastest. The commit also notes events/s per core drops as scheduler threads are added. Benchmark code (tests/bench/iopipes.c, run-pipes.php, phenom.R) is public, but no charts or later numbers are checked in. Archived 2019-03-09 (README points to folly); last code commit January 2016. The README itself gives no numbers. Category event-loops-io belongs to wave 5, not one of wave 11's categories.

notes: Numbers match the commit message exactly, but the record wrongly said the descriptor count was unstated: the commands are 'iopipes.t -n 1024 -c 1' (1024 socketpairs). Keep at C; shortcomings: first-party single-run gut check, no hardware/compiler/libevent version, libevent driven with non-persistent events (no EV_PERSIST), only 1.07x on OSX, archived since 2019.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed EuroSys 2017 paper (checked into the repo as doc/nvthreads-eurosys.pdf) compares NVthreads with Atlas and Mnemosyne on stated hardware (2x Xeon X5650, Ubuntu 14.04, Linux 3.16.7), and the eval/ and apps/ code is public, but the paper states no compiler version or flags, so it falls short of A.

corrections.workload: Making multi-threaded programs durable on emulated NVM (modified tmpfs on DRAM adding a 1,000 ns delay to each 4 KB page write): 14 Phoenix and PARSEC benchmarks with 12 threads against pthreads, DThreads and Atlas (Atlas could not run canneal or dedup); a microbenchmark that allocates 1000 pages (4 MB) and has 4 threads modify a random fraction (5%-100%) of each page, against Atlas and Mnemosyne; PageRank on the Slashdot graph (82K vertices, 950K edges) against Atlas and Mnemosyne, and on the 1.2 GB LiveJournal graph against Atlas only (Mnemosyne could not run it).
corrections.claimed_speedup: EuroSys 2017 paper: 'NVthreads is 2x-10x faster than Mnemosyne and more than 2x faster than Atlas'; 'in 10 out of the 12 workloads on which Atlas ran, NVthreads is from 7% to 100x faster depending upon the workload' (about 7% and 50% slower than Atlas on streamcluster and reverse index); microbenchmark 'NVthreads is 3x-30x faster than these systems' (Mnemosyne and Atlas 70x to over 200x slower than pthreads, NVthreads 25x down to 5x slower). PageRank on the Slashdot graph at 12 cores: 170 ms per iteration vs 500 ms Atlas (about 2.9x, derived from page data) and 5 s Mnemosyne (about 29x, derived from page data; the paper's prose says '10x faster than Mnemosyne'); LiveJournal: 5 s vs 29 s for Atlas, 'almost 6x faster', while the pthreads version takes under 1 s per iteration. Against plain pthreads NVthreads is slower: 9 of 14 apps under 28% overhead, but reverse index (5.5x), canneal (4.1x), dedup (6.7x) and ferret (4.8x) are over 4x.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper; the library's src/Makefile builds with g++ -g -m64 -msse2 -O3 -DNDEBUG -shared -fPIC -DLOCK_OWNERSHIP -DDETERM_MEMORY_ALLOC (compiler version unstated).
corrections.caveats: The baselines are other research persistence systems (Atlas, Mnemosyne), not std::thread or pthreads; NVthreads is slower than unmodified pthreads (over 4x on four PARSEC/Phoenix apps, about 5x on LiveJournal PageRank), so it is not faster than the category incumbent. NVM is emulated with software delays; Atlas could not run canneal and dedup, Mnemosyne ran only the microbenchmark and the small Slashdot PageRank graph (it crashes above 4 MB of durable data), and Mnemosyne's constant 2 s fork/pmalloc overhead was excluded. The paper's prose ratio for Mnemosyne on Slashdot (10x) does not match its own 170 ms vs 5 s figures (about 29x). Compiler flags for the benchmark applications are not stated in the paper. The root COPYING is GPL-2.0 (copyleft for a drop-in pthreads replacement) while the awesome-cpp listing says LGPL-2.1, and third-parties/ vendors Atlas, Mnemosyne and DThreads under their own licenses. The README calls it a research prototype under development, not for production. Category thread-pools-work-stealing is the closest wave-11 fit; the project is really persistent-memory threading.

notes: All quoted figures appear in the paper PDF; small fixes: LiveJournal PageRank was against Atlas only, and the paper's prose says 10x (not the derived 29x) over Mnemosyne on Slashdot. Keep at B with shortcomings: off-baseline (research systems, not pthreads), slower than pthreads, emulated NVM, GPL-2.0, abandoned since 2017-08-02.
